This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass 🌿

💡 The idea in one breath

Most weather apps keep you scrolling. PLOT does the opposite. 📵➡️🌱

You pick a place (or share your location 📍). Real weather loads 🌦️. TabPFN, an open tabular foundation model 🧠, reads your day like a row in a frost table and answers:

⏸️ Wait · 🚶 Walk · 🌿 Garden

Then it hands you three concrete steps and expects you to leave. The screen's job is under a minute. ⏱️
🚀 Live demo plot-touch-grass.onrender.com
💻 Source github.com/PranjalManhgaye/plot-touch-grass

Field Value

🌦️ Weather Open-Meteo ERA5 reanalysis + live forecast
☁️ Hosting Render free tier
⚡ Stack FastAPI, static UI, no chat layer

👥 Who it's for: anyone with a yard, balcony, or park nearby who overthinks the forecast and under-leaves the house.

articles.title: Node.js 26's default Temporal API fixes a one-hour DST drift that Date still has
articles.description: Node.js 26 enables the Temporal API with no flag. I found it fixes a real one-hour DST drift in naive Date arithmetic, but costs about 19 times more than Date per operation, and its default overflow mode doesn't throw where I expected it to.
articles.body_html:
tomorrow = new Date(now.getTime() + 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000) is a line that turns up in a lot of scheduling and billing code. It looks harmless, and for most of the year it is. Twice a year, in any timezone that observes daylight saving, it's wrong by an hour.

Node.js 26, released in May, turns on the Temporal API without a flag. The release notes describe it as a "modern date/time API for JavaScript that provides a more robust and feature-rich alternative to the legacy Date object." I pulled the official image, ran the naive pattern next to Temporal.ZonedDateTime.add(), and the drift showed up on the first try.

I wanted to know what that default actually buys a working codebase, not just what the API looks like in isolation, so everything below is a real run against the official node:26 and node:24 images, not a reading of the spec.

The drift, measured

I picked the 2026 US spring-forward (2026-03-08, clocks in America/New_York jump from 02:00 to 03:00) and started both calculations from the same instant: 2026-03-07 at 22:00 local time.

const TZ = 'America/New_York';
const startUtcMs = Date.parse('2026-03-08T03:00:00.000Z'); // 22:00 local, pre-jump

// the naive "add a day" pattern
const naiveNextDayMs = startUtcMs + 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000;

// Temporal's calendar-aware equivalent
const zdt = Temporal.Instant.fromEpochMilliseconds(startUtcMs).toZonedDateTimeISO(TZ);
const nextDay = zdt.add({ days: 1 });
result
start (local wall clock) 03/07/2026, 22:00:00
Date + 24h, read back as local time 03/08/2026, 23:00:00
Temporal zdt.add({days: 1}) 2026-03-08T*22:00:00*-04:00

The Date version lands an hour later than it should, because adding 24 hours of UTC time walks straight through the hour that the clocks skipped. Temporal keeps the wall-clock time fixed at 22:00 and lets the UTC offset move from -05:00 to -04:00 instead, which is what "the same time, one calendar day later" actually means to a person. That's the whole value proposition in one run, and it's the first thing that didn't need three attempts to show up.

What it costs you per call

Correct math isn't free. I ran a million iterations of "take an instant, add a second to it, read a field back" for both APIs, three times each, on an otherwise idle container:

trial Date (ms) Temporal (ms)
1 65.4 2071.5
2 72.8 1839.7
3 66.5 1913.1

Roughly 27 times slower, consistently, not a one-off. That number felt too clean, so I split the loop to find out which half of the operation was actually responsible, rather than trust the combined figure.

// add-only, no field read
for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) sum += inst.add({ seconds: i }).epochMilliseconds;

Isolated, .add() alone was 59.6ms for Date against 1152.9ms for Temporal — about 19 times slower on its own. Reading a field off an already-built ZonedDateTime (zdt.hour) was a smaller gap, 11.5ms against 71.9ms. So the earlier combined number wasn't an artefact of my timing window catching something unrelated; .add() really is the expensive part, and it's expensive by design, not by my mistake. Temporal objects are immutable and carry full calendar and timezone context through every operation, where Date is just a wrapped 64-bit number.

The overflow behaviour I assumed wrong

I went in expecting Temporal to be the strict, no-silent-surprises alternative to Date's habit of normalising invalid input. new Date(2026, 1, 30) quietly becomes March 2nd, because February doesn't have a 30th day and Date just keeps counting. I assumed Temporal.PlainDate.from() would refuse that outright.

new Date(2026, 1, 30).toISOString().slice(0, 10)
// '2026-03-02'

Temporal.PlainDate.from({ year: 2026, month: 2, day: 30 })
// 2026-02-28 -- no error

It doesn't throw. The default overflow mode is "constrain", which clips the out-of-range day down to the last valid one instead of raising anything. It's a different kind of wrong to Date's (clipping to the 28th is arguably more defensible than rolling into March), but it is still silent, and that contradicted what I expected walking in. Getting a real error needs an explicit option:

Temporal.PlainDate.from({ year: 2026, month: 2, day: 30 }, { overflow: 'reject' })
// Uncaught RangeError: Temporal error: day value is not in a valid range.

A genuinely malformed string throws without needing that option, so the strictness is there, just not where I first looked for it:

Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-13-40')
// RangeError: Temporal error: Parsed month value not in a valid range.

Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from('2026-01-01T00:00:00+00:00[Europe/Nonexistent]')
// RangeError: Temporal error: Unknown time zone identifier

If any of your code treats "no exception" as "the date was valid," Temporal's default construction from a plain object won't give you that for free. You still need overflow: 'reject'.

Everything prior to Node 26 still needs a flag

Node 24, the LTS line Node 26 will eventually replace, doesn't have Temporal at all without an explicit opt-in:

$ node -e "Temporal.Now.instant()"
ReferenceError: Temporal is not defined

Adding --harmony-temporal on Node 24.21.0 gets you the same global, and in my checks it behaved identically to Node 26's default — same overflow rules, same error text, same arithmetic results. So the actual change in 26 is narrower than "Temporal arrived": it was already there, behind a flag, since at least the 24.x line, sitting on V8 13.6. What 26 changes is who gets it without reading the release notes first, and it comes bundled with the V8 jump to 14.6 rather than a Temporal-specific rewrite. The flag works the other way too: Node 26 exposes --no-harmony-temporal if you need Temporal to stay undefined, which matters if a library you depend on polyfills the name and would conflict with the native one.

I also checked whether there's anything to watch while this runs in production — a counter, a log line, a flag you can read back at runtime. process.features doesn't mention it at all, and process.config.variables does list v8_enable_temporal_support and v8_enable_temporal_systemicu, both 1 on the official image — but those are compile-time build flags, not a live state: they stayed 1 even when I ran the same process with --no-harmony-temporal, which does turn the global off. So neither surfaces the actual runtime toggle. The only reliable check from inside a process is typeof Temporal, which is a reasonable thing to assert in a startup health check if you're migrating code onto it deliberately.

No startup tax for the part you don't use

Turning a global on by default raised an obvious question: does every Node 26 process now pay for Temporal even if it never touches it? I spawned twenty bare node -e "1" processes with the default flags and twenty more with --no-harmony-temporal, timing each with process.hrtime.bigint() around the spawn:

min median mean
default (Temporal on) 22.99ms 28.59ms 29.24ms
--no-harmony-temporal 24.93ms 31.65ms 30.78ms
difference within noise within noise within noise

No measurable gap, and if anything the "off" runs were marginally slower, which is noise, not a real effect. That lines up with the per-operation cost I measured above: you pay for Temporal when you call it, not for having it switched on.

What I got wrong on the way

My first version of the performance benchmark folded the field read (.toZonedDateTimeISO('UTC').hour) into the same loop as the .add() call, for both Date and Temporal. The combined number — 27x — was real, but I couldn't tell from it whether the slowdown was in the arithmetic or in extracting a usable value afterwards, and a reader could reasonably ask the same thing. Splitting the two apart (the add-only and field-only benchmarks above) was the right move: it showed .add() carries almost all of the cost, and it meant I wasn't reporting a number I couldn't explain.

Run it yourself

Everything above ran against the official node:26 and node:24 Docker images.

docker pull node:26
docker pull node:24

# the DST drift
cat > dst.js <<'EOF'
const TZ = 'America/New_York';
const startUtcMs = Date.parse('2026-03-08T03:00:00.000Z');
console.log('naive +24h:', new Date(startUtcMs + 86400000)
  .toLocaleString('en-US', { timeZone: TZ, hour12: false }));
const zdt = Temporal.Instant.fromEpochMilliseconds(startUtcMs).toZonedDateTimeISO(TZ);
console.log('Temporal add({days:1}):', zdt.add({ days: 1 }).toString());
EOF
docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/work -w /work node:26 node dst.js

# Temporal behind a flag on 24, same result as 26's default
docker run --rm node:24 node --harmony-temporal -e \
  "console.log(Temporal.Now.instant().toString())"
docker run --rm node:24 node -e "Temporal.Now.instant()"   # throws without the flag

A grep for 86400000 or 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000 in a billing or scheduling codebase takes about five minutes, and the measured gap above is the reason to spend it: anywhere that pattern adds a calendar day rather than a fixed span of milliseconds, it will be wrong on the next DST boundary it crosses, by exactly the hour I measured. Rewriting one into Temporal is a small change; finding them all is the part that takes longer than five minutes in practice.

Don't rewrite a hot path on the strength of this post alone, though. A log parser or a bulk date-range walk doing this a few million times a run will feel the 19x, and Date is still correct for anything measured in raw milliseconds rather than calendar days — the bug only shows up when you cross a DST boundary doing day-level arithmetic, which most timestamp processing never does. And if you do reach for Temporal.PlainDate.from() to validate user input, pass overflow: 'reject' by hand. Without it, a bad day gets clipped rather than flagged, and I'd have shipped that assumption wrong if I hadn't checked it directly.

articles.title: Node.js 24 Built-In SQLite: Replacing better-sqlite3 in Scripts and Edge Workers Without a Native Module
articles.description: Node.js 24 ships with native SQLite support. Understand when the built-in node:sqlite module can replace better-sqlite3 in production scripts and edge workers, and when the native module still wins.
articles.body_html:
Node.js 24 Built-In SQLite: Replacing better-sqlite3 in Scripts and Edge Workers Without a Native Module

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Most SQLite integration problems in Node.js stem from the gap between needing a simple embedded database and the friction of compiling native modules. Teams reach for better-sqlite3 because it solves the synchronous API problem, but the build step introduces deployment headaches. Cross-compilation breaks. Docker images balloon. Edge worker environments reject native binaries outright.

Node.js 24 ships with node:sqlite, a built-in module that exposes SQLite without requiring a native dependency. The module runs queries, manages transactions, and handles schema migrations using the same synchronous patterns developers already rely on.

The built-in module eliminates the compilation step. Teams write scripts that run immediately on any Node.js 24 runtime without a build phase. Edge workers accept the code because the SQLite engine ships inside the Node.js binary itself.

This matters because deployment complexity compounds. A single native dependency multiplies into platform-specific builds, architecture matrices, and runtime version locks. The built-in module collapses that matrix to zero.

Key Takeaways

  • Node.js 24 includes node:sqlite, a native SQLite module that requires no compilation or external dependencies.
  • The built-in module provides synchronous query execution and transaction support, matching the core API patterns of better-sqlite3.
  • Scripts and edge workers gain immediate compatibility because the SQLite engine ships inside the Node.js binary.
  • Feature gaps exist: better-sqlite3 offers user-defined functions, custom aggregates, and fine-grained performance tuning that node:sqlite does not yet support.
  • Migration paths depend on whether the codebase relies on better-sqlite3's advanced hooks or simply needs basic CRUD and transaction semantics.

The Legacy Landscape: Why better-sqlite3 Dominated

Developers adopted better-sqlite3 because the alternative, node-sqlite3, forced asynchronous APIs onto a database that operates synchronously.

SQLite runs on the same thread as the caller. Every query blocks until completion. Wrapping that in Promises or callbacks adds overhead without architectural benefit. The mismatch shows up in transaction code. An asynchronous wrapper turns a three-statement atomic operation into callback nesting or async/await ceremony that obscures the transactional boundary.

better-sqlite3 exposed the synchronous reality directly. Transactions became readable. Statements returned results immediately. The library compiled a native module, but the API aligned with how SQLite actually works.

The compilation requirement created the only friction point. Teams running CI pipelines hit build failures when Python or build-essential packages were missing. Dockerfile layers grew to accommodate the toolchain. Edge environments like Cloudflare Workers rejected the native binary outright.

That tradeoff made sense when no alternative existed. The API clarity justified the deployment cost. Node.js 24 changes the equation by offering synchronous SQLite access without the native module penalty.

node:sqlite API Deep Dive: Opening Databases and Running Queries

The node:sqlite module ships as part of the Node.js standard library. Import it the same way as node:fs or node:path.

import { DatabaseSync } from 'node:sqlite';

const db = new DatabaseSync(':memory:');

The constructor accepts a file path or the special :memory: token for in-memory databases. No options object. No compilation step. The database opens immediately.

Running queries requires preparing a statement and executing it. The two-step pattern prevents SQL injection and allows parameter binding.

const stmt = db.prepare('CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT)');
stmt.run();

const insert = db.prepare('INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES (?)');
insert.run('Alice');
insert.run('Bob');

const select = db.prepare('SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?');
const rows = select.all('Alice');
console.log(rows); // [{ id: 1, name: 'Alice' }]

The .run() method executes statements that do not return rows. The .all() method retrieves every matching row as an array. The .get() method returns the first row or undefined.

Transactions wrap multiple statements in an atomic block. Roll back if any operation fails.

const insertTx = db.prepare('INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES (?)');

db.exec('BEGIN TRANSACTION');
try {
  insertTx.run('Charlie');
  insertTx.run('Diana');
  db.exec('COMMIT');
} catch (err) {
  db.exec('ROLLBACK');
  throw err;
}

The API surface matches better-sqlite3 at the statement level. Developers familiar with .prepare(), .run(), and .all() carry that knowledge directly into node:sqlite code. The difference shows up in what the module omits, not in what it changes.

Feature Parity Check: What better-sqlite3 Had That node:sqlite Does Not

better-sqlite3 offers features that node:sqlite does not yet implement. The gap matters when advanced use cases depend on those capabilities.

User-defined functions let developers register JavaScript callbacks that SQLite can invoke inside queries. A better-sqlite3 codebase might register a slugify() function and call it directly in a SELECT statement. node:sqlite does not expose the sqlite3_create_function() binding.

Custom aggregates extend SQLite's built-in SUM() and AVG() with application-specific logic. Teams implementing weighted averages or geometric means rely on the aggregate API. The built-in module does not support it.

The backup API provides hot-copy functionality for live databases. Scripts that snapshot production data mid-operation use db.backup() to avoid locking the source file. node:sqlite lacks the method.

Pragma shortcuts simplify configuration. better-sqlite3 exposes db.pragma('journal_mode = WAL') as a first-class method. The built-in module requires executing raw SQL: db.exec('PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL').

Column type introspection reveals schema metadata at runtime. A migration tool might inspect existing column types before altering a table. better-sqlite3 returns type information from prepared statements. node:sqlite does not expose the underlying sqlite3_column_type() call.

The feature set aligns with the module's design goal. Node.js 24 targets the common path: CRUD operations, transactions, and schema management. Advanced hooks remain the domain of third-party libraries.

Migrating Scripts and Edge Workers: Real-World Replacement Patterns

Scripts that rely on better-sqlite3 for straightforward data persistence migrate cleanly to node:sqlite. The pattern holds when the codebase uses prepared statements, parameter binding, and transactions without touching user-defined functions or aggregates.

A typical migration replaces the import and constructor, then verifies that statement methods map directly.

// Before: better-sqlite3
import Database from 'better-sqlite3';
const db = new Database('data.db');

// After: node:sqlite
import { DatabaseSync } from 'node:sqlite';
const db = new DatabaseSync('data.db');

The statement API remains identical for .prepare(), .run(), .get(), and .all(). Code that binds parameters with ? placeholders or named bindings works unchanged.

const insert = db.prepare('INSERT INTO logs (message, level) VALUES (?, ?)');
insert.run('Application started', 'INFO');

const query = db.prepare('SELECT * FROM logs WHERE level = ?');
const rows = query.all('ERROR');

Edge workers running on platforms like Cloudflare Workers or Vercel Edge Functions gain immediate compatibility. These environments reject native binaries but accept standard library modules. A worker that previously failed to deploy because better-sqlite3 required compilation now runs without modification.

The tradeoff surfaces when the script relies on better-sqlite3 features outside the core API. A logging tool that registers a custom format_timestamp() SQL function must rewrite that logic as JavaScript post-processing. A backup script that uses db.backup() must switch to copying the database file at the filesystem level.

Migration assessment reduces to a feature audit. Grep the codebase for .function(), .aggregate(), .backup(), and .pragma(). If those methods appear, the script requires either refactoring or staying on better-sqlite3. If the codebase only calls .prepare(), .run(), .get(), and .all(), the switch is mechanical.

Performance and Stability: Benchmarks and Production Readiness

The performance characteristics of node:sqlite match better-sqlite3 because both modules link against the same SQLite engine. Query execution time depends on the SQL itself, not the binding layer. A well-indexed SELECT runs identically in both environments.

Prepared statement overhead measures in microseconds. The difference between the two modules falls within measurement noise for typical workloads. A benchmark running 10,000 inserts in a transaction shows less than 5% variance between node:sqlite and better-sqlite3.

The stability concern centers on module maturity. better-sqlite3 has shipped production releases since 2016. The API surface is stable. Edge cases have been identified and fixed. node:sqlite entered the standard library in Node.js 22 as experimental and stabilized in Node.js 24. The module has less real-world mileage.

Production readiness depends on risk tolerance and use case. A build script that generates static site data from a database can adopt node:sqlite immediately. The worst-case failure mode is a broken build, not lost user data. A long-running application server that handles financial transactions should wait for broader ecosystem adoption and stability reports.

The module does not introduce new failure modes beyond what SQLite itself allows. Database corruption, disk full errors, and constraint violations surface the same way in both libraries. The binding layer does not add retry logic or error recovery. Developers handle errors at the application level.

Monitoring requirements do not change. Track query execution time, transaction volume, and database file size the same way regardless of binding. The built-in module does not expose performance metrics beyond what SQLite's EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN provides.

When to Keep better-sqlite3 vs When to Switch

The decision matrix collapses to three factors: feature requirements, deployment environment, and maintenance burden.

Codebases that register JavaScript functions for use inside SQL queries must stay on better-sqlite3. The API does not have a node:sqlite equivalent. Rewriting those queries to pull data into JavaScript and apply transformations there changes the architecture and often degrades performance.

Aggregates that compute custom metrics across rows similarly require better-sqlite3. A query that calculates a percentile rank using a JavaScript aggregate function has no direct translation to the built-in module.

Deployment to edge workers flips the equation. Platforms that reject native binaries make better-sqlite3 unusable. The choice becomes node:sqlite or no SQLite at all. Scripts running in serverless functions on AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Functions, or Azure Functions gain faster cold starts by eliminating the native module. The reduction in deployment package size shortens upload time and improves function initialization.

Teams maintaining multiple projects with different Node.js versions face a version lock decision. better-sqlite3 runs on Node.js 14 and later. node:sqlite requires Node.js 24. A monorepo with services on different runtime versions cannot standardize on the built-in module until every service upgrades.

The maintenance burden calculation compares ongoing dependency updates against version lock risk. better-sqlite3 releases quarterly. Each update requires rebuilding native binaries and testing across platforms. node:sqlite updates arrive with Node.js releases. The module version stays synchronized with the runtime version. Teams already managing Node.js upgrades absorb the SQLite update as part of that process.

Libraries published to npm that depend on SQLite should continue using better-sqlite3. The library's broader Node.js compatibility ensures users on older runtimes can still install the package. A CLI tool that supports Node.js 18 cannot require Node.js 24 just to enable SQLite.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does node:sqlite support WAL mode?

Yes. Execute db.exec('PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL') after opening the database. The module does not provide a shortcut method, but the pragma works identically to better-sqlite3.

Can I use node:sqlite in production applications today?

The module is stable in Node.js 24. Production readiness depends on the application's risk profile. Build tools, scripts, and edge workers are good candidates. Mission-critical transaction systems should wait for broader ecosystem validation.

Will better-sqlite3 continue to receive updates?

The library remains actively maintained. Teams that rely on user-defined functions, custom aggregates, or older Node.js versions will continue using better-sqlite3 regardless of the built-in module's availability.

How do I migrate a database from better-sqlite3 to node:sqlite?

No migration is necessary. Both modules read and write standard SQLite database files. Copy the .db file and open it with the new module. Schema and data remain compatible.

Does node:sqlite work with TypeScript?

Yes. The module ships with type definitions in Node.js 24. Import DatabaseSync from node:sqlite and TypeScript infers statement return types automatically.

Conclusion: Native SQLite and the Future of Embedded Databases in Node.js

Node.js 24's built-in SQLite module eliminates the native dependency barrier for the majority of embedded database use cases. Scripts that execute queries, manage transactions, and handle schema changes now run without compilation steps or platform-specific binaries. Edge workers gain access to persistent storage without violating runtime constraints.

The feature gap between node:sqlite and better-sqlite3 defines the boundary. Projects that rely on user-defined functions, custom aggregates, or advanced introspection must stay on the native module. Straightforward CRUD applications, build tools, and serverless functions switch immediately.

The long-term trajectory favors the built-in module. As Node.js releases continue, the standard library API will expand based on real-world usage patterns. The ecosystem will converge on node:sqlite for new projects while maintaining better-sqlite3 for specialized requirements.

That covers the essential patterns for adopting Node.js 24's native SQLite support. Evaluate your feature requirements, audit your deployment environment, and apply the built-in module where it fits. The difference in deployment complexity will be immediate.

articles.title: Day 7 of Building Crowdwide — UI Polishing, My First Advertiser, and Translation Breaking AGAIN 😭
articles.description: First of all, THANK YOU for this progress and reading my articles! ❤️  Welcome back to another update...
articles.body_html:
First of all, THANK YOU for this progress and reading my articles! ❤️

Welcome back to another update on building Crowdwide, my social platform!

A lot has happened since my last update. I'm working on polishing the UI, improving the Waves system, getting my first external advertiser, welcoming a new moderator, and trying to fix a translation feature that keeps breaking for some reason. 😭

So yeah, there's a lot to talk about. Let's get into it!

1. Current Progress 📊

Here's where Crowdwide stands right now:

  • 7 members
  • 35 posts
  • 4 communities
  • 2 advertisers, including me

I know these numbers are still small, but I'm happy that people are starting to join and try the platform!

Every little bit of progress matters, especially when you're building something on your own with a budget of basically ZERO (I'm not harmed by this line). 😂

I'm still at the early stage, and I know there's a long way to go. But getting actual people to try something you've built yourself feels different from just seeing it work on your own computer.

2. My First External Advertiser! 🎉

One of the most exciting things that happened recently was getting my first external advertiser!

The advertiser submitted an application, and it was approved by both a moderator and an admin.

At that time, I was handling both the admin panel and the moderator panel myself.

But there was one problem...

The advertiser didn't have enough Waves to start their campaign. 😭

And honestly, I hadn't even thought about this situation properly before.

Here's how the advertising process works on Crowdwide:

  1. An advertiser submits their website, product, or service details along with a description.
  2. The campaign goes through moderator and admin approval.
  3. Once approved, the advertiser needs to set a campaign budget of at least 25 Waves.
  4. The campaign can then run, with Waves being charged according to impressions and clicks.

The idea is to make promotion accessible to people who want to reach an audience without needing a huge advertising budget.

Now, here's what actually happened.

I approved the advertiser's application, but I didn't focus on whether they had enough Waves to launch the campaign.

I even emailed them twice because I was wondering what was going on. I thought, What's the matter? Why aren't they starting their campaign?

Then I checked the details and finally realized...

THEY DIDN'T HAVE THE 25 WAVES NEEDED TO START THE CAMPAIGN!

That's why the campaign was paused.

I had been wondering why they seemed busy, when the actual problem was something I hadn't considered in the first place. 😭

This was a good lesson for me: approving an advertiser's application is only one part of the process. The advertiser also needs to be able to fund the campaign with enough internal Waves to get started.

Crowdwide is still in its early stages, so the audience is small right now. I'm hoping that changes as more people join!

3. The Waves System 🌊

After this happened, Harun( @koda2026 ) suggested giving an approved advertiser a one-time boost of 25 Waves so they could try launching a campaign.

That got me thinking...

Instead of helping only one advertiser, I decided to give 25 Waves to every current user account as a one-time early-user boost!

This should give early users a little more room to explore the platform and try its features.

I also realized that I need to think more carefully about how people get their first Waves, especially when some features require Waves before users can fully try them.

But I want to clarify something important:

Waves are an internal platform currency. They are NOT real money, NOT cryptocurrency, and NOT connected to a bank account.

They are designed to help users participate in Crowdwide's internal reward and promotion systems.

Since I'm under 18 and building this project with a very limited budget, I wanted to experiment with an internal system rather than deal with real-money payments.

The goal is to make the platform's reward and promotion features accessible without requiring users to make real-money payments just to participate in this internal economy.

How can users earn Waves?

Here's the current reward structure:

Activity Waves Reward
Creating a post 1–3 Waves
Creating a comment 1–3 Waves
Receiving likes 0.1–1 Wave
Receiving comments 0.1–1 Wave
Joining a community 1–2 Waves
Creating a community 2–5 Waves
Completing a quest 1–5 Waves

These rewards are intended to encourage participation and help users explore different parts of Crowdwide.

Waves can also be used for promotions and other supported platform features.

I'm still learning how to balance the reward system so it feels useful without making it too easy to abuse.

I want people to have reasons to participate, but I also need to make sure the system isn't easily exploited by people trying to collect rewards without genuinely using the platform.

That's something I'll keep improving as Crowdwide grows.

4. A New Moderator Joins Crowdwide! 🛡️

Another important update: Harun( @koda2026 ) agreed to help moderate Crowdwide! 🎉

I'm really grateful for this because building a platform alone means you have to think about everything yourself: features, UI, bugs, moderation, rewards, advertising, and about a million other things.

Having someone else look at the platform and give honest feedback helps a lot.

Harun also gave me some useful suggestions about separating moderation actions according to their risk.

Here's the general approach I'm working toward.

Lower-risk moderator actions:

  • Mark a post as a “Good post.”
  • Propose an edit to a post.
  • Flag obvious spam so it can be automatically hidden while awaiting final review.

Higher-risk actions requiring admin approval:

  • Warn or suspend a user.
  • Permanently delete a post.
  • Change community settings.

The idea is to let moderators handle routine tasks while keeping more serious actions under tighter control.

I don't want moderators to be powerless, but I also don't want one person to have too much control over the platform.

Some actions are simple and reversible, while others can seriously affect a user's account or community. It makes sense to treat them differently.

I'm still working on improving the moderation system, but this feedback gave me a clearer direction.

Welcome aboard, Harun! 🎉 And thank you for the suggestions!

5. UI Polishing Is Taking FOREVER 😭

Now comes the part I've been spending a lot of time on: polishing the user interface.

Crowdwide has more than 80 pages, and I still have around 30 or more pages left to polish.

BRO, WHY ARE THERE SO MANY PAGES? 😭

I thought adding features was the big challenge, but now I'm going through all these pages and finding things that could be clearer, better organized, or more consistent.

And honestly, this process has taught me a lot about UI design.

I'm learning things like:

  • Keeping interfaces simple and clear.
  • Using bold text to highlight important information.
  • Improving spacing between elements.
  • Organizing headings, subheadings, and content properly.
  • Making layouts more consistent.
  • Improving alignment so pages feel more organized.
  • Making information easier to scan instead of putting everything in front of the user at once.

Sometimes, a page technically works, but it still doesn't feel right.

The buttons work, the information is there, and the feature does what it's supposed to do. But the page can still feel cluttered or confusing.

That's why I'm trying to focus on more than just functionality. I want Crowdwide to feel understandable and comfortable to use, too.

I'm also trying to avoid unnecessary backend calls. I already have a preloader, and I don't want to add unnecessary work for the server just to make the interface feel more polished.

Since I'm using free-tier hosting, performance is something I have to keep in mind as well.

I can't just throw money at better hosting, so I have to work with what I've got. 😂

For now, I'm focusing on improving the existing pages instead of endlessly adding new features.

6. Helping Early Advertisers

The first advertiser situation also got me thinking about how difficult it can be to start advertising on a platform that doesn't have a large audience yet.

Since Crowdwide is still new, advertisers might not get much reach right now.

That's understandable. A platform with only a handful of members can't offer the same audience as a huge established social network.

So I'm considering giving early advertisers some Waves from my own account to help them test their campaigns.

Harun's suggestion about the one-time 25-Waves boost made me think more about how to help people get started.

I don't want someone to go through the application process, get approved, and then discover that they can't launch a campaign because they don't have enough Waves.

At the same time, I need to keep the system fair and make sure the rules are clear.

I also want to keep track of transfers and make sure the system has proper abuse detection.

If Waves are transferred between accounts, I want those transfers to be recorded properly so I can understand where the Waves are going and investigate anything suspicious.

Transparency and abuse prevention are important, especially when a reward system is involved. I made the system for it.

I want the Waves economy to be useful, but I also want to understand how it's being used and keep improving it as the platform grows.


and yea, my system detected that... someone has to give those 179waves to system basic to make him neutral!!

At this point, I'm basically considering taking a loan from myself. 💀😂

7. Translation Is Broken AGAIN!! 😭

Okay, this one is frustrating.

I noticed that the translation feature stopped working again, and I honestly don't know why.

At first, I tried integrating Google Translate using its developer documentation.

But after going through the setup, I found out that the option I was trying to use required payment or billing setup.

SORRY SUNDAR PICHAI (CEO OF GOOGLE), MY BUDGET IS LOW (OR YOU CAN SAY 0) LOL 😂

Then I tried another service, thinking maybe I could get a smaller plan or a little free trial.

BUT THEY ASKED FOR MONEY TOO!!

I SAID NO AGAIN. 😭

Then I asked Claude for help, and somehow it got the translation feature working! It also refactored some of my code.

And guess what?

TRANSLATION WORKED FOR SOME TIME...

I checked again later, and it was BROKEN AGAIN!! 😭😭

I genuinely don't know what's causing it.

Is it an API issue? A configuration problem? Something in my implementation? Did something get changed during the refactoring?

I haven't figured it out yet.

I'm almost done with this feature, and I really want to get it working properly. I don't want to abandon it after putting so much effort into it.

So I'm asking for help from the community.

If you've worked with translation APIs, multilingual features, or debugging API integrations, could you help me figure out what's going wrong?

Even a suggestion about what to check first would be useful.

Here's the repository:

https://github.com/DeveloperPuneet/Crowdwide

And here's the live platform:

https://www.crowdwide.run.place/

If you're willing to take a look or have any ideas, please let me know!

Any help, suggestions, or guidance would genuinely mean a lot to me. ❤️

8. Video Tutorials Might Be Coming (Not sure) 🎥

I'm also thinking about creating some short video tutorials to make Crowdwide easier to understand.

Even if a platform has useful features, people might not know how to use them when they first arrive.

I could make short tutorials covering things like:

  • How to create an account.
  • How to create posts on the main feed and inside communities.
  • How communities work.
  • How to use quests and events.
  • How the Waves system works.
  • How to create an advertising campaign. and adding them in docs maybe useful for someone... The idea is to make it easier for new users to understand the platform without having to figure everything out by clicking around.

I haven't made these videos yet, so this is still a plan rather than something that's already available.

But I think tutorials could be useful as Crowdwide grows and more people start trying its features.

9. Crowdwide Spotlight? 👀

Another idea I've been thinking about is something called Crowdwide Spotlight.

The idea is to let people share links to their external reviews, along with a short description.

For example, someone could share a link to a review they've published elsewhere and add a little context about what it's about.

It could give users another way to share their work and help others discover useful content outside Crowdwide.

I'm still thinking about how exactly it should work, so this is just an idea for now. But I already created a community named Crowdwide Spotlight on Crowdwide and you can post there...

I don't want to rush into implementing it before I have a clearer idea of how it would fit into the platform.

For now, it's on my list of things to explore later.

10. What's Next for Crowdwide? 🚀

There are still quite a few things I want to work on.

My current priorities are:

  • UI polishing: Continue working through the remaining pages and make the interface clearer and more consistent.
  • Translation: Figure out why the translation feature keeps breaking and get it working reliably.
  • Waves system: Keep improving the reward system, transfer tracking, and abuse detection.
  • Advertising: Make it easier for approved advertisers to understand what they need to launch a campaign.
  • Moderation: Continue improving moderator tools and safeguards for higher-risk actions.
  • Crowdwide Spotlight: Think through the idea before deciding how to implement it. (community is already there... you can post and build it)

There are plenty of things to do, but I'm trying to take them one step at a time.

I don't want to keep adding features forever without making the existing ones better.

At this stage, improving what I've already built is just as important as building something new.

11. I'd Love Your Feedback! ❤️

First of all, thank you again to everyone who has read my updates, checked out Crowdwide, offered suggestions, or supported this project in any way.

I'm building Crowdwide with a very limited budget, and I'm learning a lot as I go.

Some things work, some things break, and sometimes I discover a problem only after someone tries to use a feature. That's part of building something new, I guess. 😂

There are definitely things I still need to improve, and honest feedback helps me figure out what to focus on.

I'd especially love to hear your thoughts on a few things:

  • The Waves reward system: Do the reward ranges seem reasonable? Are there any obvious ways people might abuse it?
  • Advertising: What could make the campaign setup easier to understand for a first-time advertiser?
  • Moderation: What other safeguards or tools should I consider?
  • Translation: If you've worked with translation APIs, could you help me figure out why mine keeps breaking?
  • UI design: What makes a social platform feel simple and easy to use?
  • General feedback: If you check out Crowdwide, what's one thing you think I should improve first?

You can check out the project here:

🌐 Live platform: https://www.crowdwide.run.place/

💻 GitHub repository: https://github.com/DeveloperPuneet/Crowdwide

I'm still at the beginning of this journey, and Crowdwide has a lot of room to grow.

But I'm excited to keep building, fixing things, learning from feedback, and seeing where this project goes.

Thank you for reading, and see you in the next update! 👋❤️

articles.title: I’m 12. I’m Building an AI Sandbox on a $150 Phone. Here’s Why I’m Trying to Break It First.
articles.description: Everyone is building AI agents right now. They are connecting them to APIs, giving them file system...
articles.body_html:
Everyone is building AI agents right now. They are connecting them to APIs, giving them file system access, and letting them write code.

But almost nobody is talking about what happens when the agent hallucinates, gets prompt-injected, or decides to run an infinite loop.

If you give an AI agent the keys to your environment, you aren't just building a feature. You are building a security risk.

I’m 12 years old, and I’m building KODA, an AI coding ecosystem. Because I build entirely on a $150 Android phone on spotty 3G, I don't have the luxury of heavy, bloated security suites. Every millisecond of CPU and every megabyte of RAM counts.

Recently, I had a deep technical discussion with a senior engineer about Docker’s new agent architecture and the "two-writer rule" for AI isolation. It completely changed how I approach KODA’s secure JavaScript sandbox.

Here is the mental model I’m using to secure AI execution, and why I’m actively trying to break my own code before anyone else does.

The Core Problem: The "Black Box" Execution

When an AI generates JavaScript code and you run it in the browser, the default behavior is to give it full access to the DOM, window, localStorage, and the network.

If the AI is tricked by a malicious prompt injection, it can:

  1. Steal the user's session tokens from localStorage.
  2. Inject malicious scripts into the DOM.
  3. Spam API endpoints until your server crashes.

You cannot trust the AI's output. Therefore, the environment it runs in must assume hostility from line one.

The Philosophy: "Break Your Own Sandbox"

A senior engineer recently gave me the best piece of security advice I’ve ever received:

"Break your own sandbox before anyone else does, and write down what fell out. The failures you publish become the spec everyone else trusts."

Most developers build a sandbox, test it with "happy path" code (like console.log("Hello World")), and call it a day.

Instead, I am treating KODA’s sandbox like a Chaos Engineering target. Before I add a new feature, I write a script specifically designed to escape the sandbox. I try to access window.parent. I try to execute an infinite while loop. I try to bypass the JSON schema validation.

If my attack script succeeds, the feature doesn't ship. Period.

How KODA Handles AI Execution (The Architecture)

Building a secure JS sandbox on a low-end mobile device requires ruthless architectural discipline. Here are the three non-negotiable rules I enforce in KODA:

1. Strict DOM and Global Isolation

The AI-generated code never touches the real window or document objects. It runs in a heavily restricted Web Worker / iframe environment. I use a Proxy to intercept any attempts to access global variables. If the code tries to read window.location, the proxy returns undefined or throws a custom error. It doesn't just fail silently; it fails loudly.

2. The "Fail Closed" Schema Validation

Before the code is even executed, the AI's output is parsed against a strict JSON schema. If the AI is supposed to return a configuration object, but it returns a function or an unexpected string, the parser rejects it immediately. We don't try to "fix" the AI's output. We reject it and ask for a retry.

3. The "Two-Writer" Rule for State

This is the biggest takeaway from my recent discussions. An AI agent should never be allowed to both propose a state change and approve it.
In KODA, the AI can generate the code (Writer 1), but the execution engine and the strict sandbox boundaries (Writer 2) decide if it's allowed to run. Separation of duties prevents self-attestation loops.

The Constraint Advantage

People think building on a $150 phone is a disadvantage. In security, it’s an unfair advantage.

When you have 4GB of RAM and a mid-tier processor, you can't afford to run heavy, redundant security checks. Every single control has to earn its place. It forces you to write lean, deterministic, and highly optimized code. You can't hide bad architecture behind a massive cloud budget.

The Takeaway

If you are building AI agents, stop asking "What can this agent do?" and start asking "What is the worst thing this agent could do, and how do I make it physically impossible?"

Don't wait for a user to find the exploit. Break your own sandbox first. Publish the failures. Build the spec.

I’m still learning, and KODA is still in development. But treating security as a daily practice, rather than an afterthought, is the only way to build tools that people can actually trust.

How are you securing your AI agents? Are you using Web Workers, iframes, or server-side sandboxes? Let’s discuss in the comments! 🐯

articles.title: I couldn't design an app icon, so I collected 18,000 real ones
articles.description: When I ship an app, the part I get stuck on is the icon, not the code.  Writing the code is the part...
articles.body_html:
When I ship an app, the part I get stuck on is the icon, not the code.

Writing the code is the part I know how to do. A blank 1024 × 1024 canvas is not.

So I stopped trying to design from nothing and started looking at what real apps do. That turned into a side project: a library of 18,491 real app icons from the App Store and Google Play.

👉 applore.app

The three bad options

When you need an icon as a solo developer, you usually get to pick one of these:

  1. Hire a designer. The right call if you have the budget. For a side project that might make $0, I usually don't.
  2. Draw it yourself. Mine look bad. I've accepted this.
  3. Ask an image model for "an app icon". You get the glossy, slightly-too-perfect look that everyone now recognizes as AI.

None of these fixed the real problem: I didn't know what a good icon for my kind of app should look like.

What actually helped

The thing that worked was boring: looking at what real apps in my category already do. Put 30 or 40 icons from the same category side by side and two things jump out. The colors that category expects, and the symbols everyone has already used.

Sometimes it's almost funny. In our library, 66% of cleaner app icons use a broom.

Doing this by hand was slow, though. The App Store doesn't let you filter by color or style, and there's no way to see what an icon looked like last year. So I started collecting them.

So I built a library

APPLORE syncs icons from the App Store and Google Play every day. Right now it has 18,491 of them (10,826 from the App Store, 7,665 from Google Play). You can browse by:

  • Color, down to the exact shade
  • Style: flat, gradient, 3D, glass, mascot, letter
  • Category, same as the stores
  • First letter, which is surprisingly handy when you're naming your app

What 18,491 icons taught me

Once everything was tagged, I could finally answer questions I used to guess at:

  • Half of all app icons have no text at all. If your idea needs a word to make sense, it probably needs a better idea.
  • 73% sit on a solid background, and two out of three are flat.
  • Light blue is the most common color (17.2% of icons), then red (13.6%), orange (11.8%) and yellow (11.7%).
  • The icons that stand out add one thing on top of a simple shape. Icons our team picked as featured are twice as likely to be 3D (12.9% vs 6.3%) and more than twice as likely to use a mascot (19.3% vs 7.5%).

My takeaway: start from what your category already looks like, so people recognize what your app does, then change one thing so it doesn't blend in.

Icons change more than I expected

When an app changes its icon, the old version stays in the library. That turned out to be one of the most fun parts to browse.

Of the 4,812 App Store apps we first recorded in September 2024, 1,464 (30.4%) had a different icon by October 2026. Almost one in three, in two years. Most of them kept the same logo and just changed the material: glossier, more depth, closer to Apple's Liquid Glass look.

The boring technical part

Search was the fun engineering problem. People type things like "a friendly owl for a language app" or search in Chinese, and keyword matching falls apart fast.

What I ended up with:

  • Each icon gets a text description (subject, style, colors, mood), and that text is turned into a 768-dimension multilingual embedding, so a Chinese query doesn't need translating first.
  • No pgvector. 18,000 vectors are only a few dozen MB, so the server loads them all into memory and does a brute-force dot product. A search takes about a dozen milliseconds.
  • The semantic results are merged with plain keyword results using reciprocal rank fusion (each list contributes 1 / (60 + rank)), so exact name matches still win when you search for an app by name.

At this size, a flat array and a loop is simpler than a vector database, and one less thing to run.

From reference to your own icon

Browsing only gets you a direction. The rest of the site is the stuff I kept doing by hand after finding one:

  • Generate an icon with AI, using a library icon as the reference, then refine it in plain words ("make it warm orange", "remove the text").
  • Preview it on a real home screen, next to system apps, in light, dark and tinted mode.
  • Export every size iOS, Android and the web need in one zip.

Browsing is free with limits (the first 300 icons in each list, 5 downloads and 5 AI searches a day). New accounts get 50 credits, which is about 10 generated icons.

What I'd love feedback on

The part I'm least sure about is browsing by color. I use it all the time, but I can't tell if it actually helps people design an icon, or if it's just nice to look at.

So two things:

  1. Do you browse by color when you design, or is it just pretty?
  2. Drop your app's icon in the comments. I'll reply to each one and tell you which patterns from the data it follows and how it holds up at home-screen size. If you want to try making one, I'll add a code for 50 free credits (about 10 AI icons).

Thanks for reading. If you're stuck on an icon right now, start here.
